question: Why are installed renewable capacity and electricity generation different indicators?
expected_behavior: Installed capacity is different from actual electricity generated. Weather, maintenance and grid constraints can reduce output below rated capacity; identify technology, unit, date and whether planned, installed or operational.
llm_response:
Short answer
- Because "capacity" is a rated or recorded potential (a number that can be planned, approved, installed or reported) while "generation" is the actual electricity produced over time — they measure different things and can diverge for several technical and reporting reasons [05_Renewable_Energy_and_Power.txt#page-2-chunk-0][05_Renewable_Energy_and_Power.txt#page-2-chunk-3].

How the indicators differ (kept separate by lifecycle stage, records/statuses, exceptions and system outcomes)

- Lifecycle stages and status labels
  - A capacity figure can be "planned", "approved", "installed" or "operational" — those stages are distinct and change what the capacity number means [05_Renewable_Energy_and_Power.txt#page-2-chunk-3].  
  - Example of stage mismatch: a rooftop system may be approved before it is installed, so an approval does not equal delivered generation capacity yet [05_Renewable_Energy_and_Power.txt#page-2-chunk-1].

- Records / measurement attributes you must check
  - Capacity claims should identify the technology, measurement unit and reporting date as well as the status (planned/installed/operational) because those details affect interpretation [05_Renewable_Energy_and_Power.txt#page-2-chunk-3].

- Exceptions and reasons actual generation differs from rated capacity
  - An installed system can produce less than its rated capacity because of weather, maintenance or grid constraints [05_Renewable_Energy_and_Power.txt#page-2-chunk-1].  
  - Variable renewables require transmission, forecasting, storage and flexible resources; without sufficient system integration, capacity may not translate into usable generation at all times [05_Renewable_Energy_and_Power.txt#page-1-chunk-13].

- System-level outcomes that separate capacity from delivered electricity
  - Energy policy must address not only building capacity but strengthening the wider power system (forecasting, storage, flexibility) so that capacity can be converted into reliable generation and supply to users [05_Renewable_Energy_and_Power.txt#page-1-chunk-13].  
  - Household adoption and access/reliability/affordability are separate indicators from installed capacity and actual generation; rooftop programmes increase local capacity but that does not automatically equal increased system-wide generation or access outcomes [05_Renewable_Energy_and_Power.txt#page-1-chunk-8][05_Renewable_Energy_and_Power.txt#page-3-chunk-4].

What the provided context does not give
- The context does not provide numerical examples, formulas (e.g., capacity factor calculations), specific verification procedures for converting capacity to expected generation, or typical magnitudes of the differences. Those details are not available in the provided excerpts.
judge_reasoning: The candidate answer accurately explains the difference between installed renewable capacity and electricity generation, aligning with the expected behavior. It correctly identifies that capacity is a potential measure while generation is the actual output, and it provides reasons for the divergence, such as weather, maintenance, and grid constraints, all supported by the source context.
